name: Chin tuck (cervical retraction)
duration_reps: 5 reps x 5 s hold (app-chosen conservative dose; CCOHS 'head glide' is 20 counts x 5-10)
steps: Start sitting or standing tall, eyes level, ears over shoulders, shoulders relaxed.
Without lifting or dropping the chin, glide the head straight back horizontally, as if making a double chin. Small, comfortable movement only.
Hold the end pose for about 5 s, breathing normally; keep the chin level.
Release slowly (about 2 s) back to neutral. Repeat.
key_cue: Slide the head back along a horizontal line, like a drawer closing.
common_mistake: Nodding the chin down to the chest, or pushing so hard the neck strains.
evidence_note: CCOHS (read) lists the head glide; CUH leaflet (read) lists chin retraction. Blanpied 2017 neck pain CPG (read) recommends exercise for people WITH neck pain with mobility deficits but does not specifically recommend chin tuck; no trial shows a desk-break chin tuck prevents pain. Dose is app-chosen.

name: Upper trapezius side-tilt stretch
duration_reps: 2 reps per side x 15-20 s hold
steps: Sit tall; hold the seat edge with the right hand (or press the right shoulder down).
Slowly tilt the left ear toward the left shoulder over about 3 s, nose forward.
Hold 15-20 s with relaxed breathing; feel a stretch on the right side of the neck.
Return slowly; switch sides. Do not pull on the head.

evidence_note: NHS 'neck stretch' (5 s holds x3), Mayo 15-30 s holds, CUH side bend. Hold times differ between sources; 15-20 s chosen as a compromise.

name: Shoulder shrug and drop
steps: Sit or stand tall, arms relaxed at sides.
Inhale and raise both shoulders toward the ears over 2 s until mild tension.
Hold 3-5 s.
Exhale and let the shoulders drop heavily, letting arms hang loose. Repeat 3 times.
key_cue: Let go completely on the drop.
common_mistake: Holding the breath; lifting so hard it hurts.
evidence_note: CCOHS recommends 3-5 s holds, 2-3 reps for early tension.

name: Backward shoulder rolls
steps: Sit or stand tall, arms relaxed.
Lift both shoulders up toward the ears.
Roll them back and then down in a large slow circle (about 3 s per roll), squeezing the blades together at the back.
Repeat 5 times, then optionally 5 forward.
key_cue: Make big, slow, smooth circles.
common_mistake: Fast tiny circles; pushing the head forward.
evidence_note: CCOHS: 5 backward then 5 forward.

name: Scapular squeeze (shoulder blade retraction)
steps: Sit tall, arms by sides or elbows bent 90 degrees, thumbs pointing outward.
Draw both shoulder blades back and slightly down, as if tucking them into back pockets, over 2 s.
Hold 5 s; chest opens; do not arch the lower back.
Release over 2 s. Repeat 10 times.
key_cue: Think 'blades toward spine', not 'shoulders up'.
common_mistake: Shrugging, flaring the ribs and arching the lower back.
evidence_note: Blanpied 2017 recommends scapulothoracic strengthening for patients with acute neck pain with mobility deficits (Grade B); it does not test or recommend this 5 s desk squeeze. CCOHS chest stretch includes the squeeze without a hold. Dose is app-chosen.

name: Doorway / wall chest (pec) stretch
posture: standing at doorway or wall corner

steps: Stand beside a doorframe or wall; raise the right arm with the elbow bent 90 degrees and just below shoulder height, forearm on the frame.
Step the right foot forward slightly and gently turn the torso away to the left.
Hold 15-20 s; feel a mild stretch across the front of the right chest/shoulder; keep ribs down.
Release; switch sides. (Alternative: hands behind head, elbows back, as in CCOHS.)
key_cue: Elbow at or just below shoulder height; keep the neck relaxed.
common_mistake: Letting the lower back arch; forcing past mild stretch.

name: Seated thoracic extension over chair back
posture: seated on chair with a back
steps: Sit tall on a chair with a supportive back; place hands behind the head (elbows wide) or cross arms on the chest.
Take a breath in and gently lean the upper back backward over the top of the chair back, lifting the chest.
Hold 3-5 s, looking forward or slightly up.
Return upright and exhale. Repeat; move the contact point up/down a few cm.
key_cue: Bend at the mid back, not the lower back or neck.
common_mistake: Throwing the head back; chair that tips or has wheels without being locked.

name: Wall angels
steps: Stand with back, hips and head close to a wall, feet 10-15 cm from the wall, knees soft.
Place arms against the wall with elbows bent 90 degrees ('goalpost').
Slowly slide the arms up the wall to overhead as far as they go without the lower back or ribs lifting off; 3 s up.
Slide back down 3 s. Repeat 8 times.
key_cue: Keep the lower back and head touching or close to the wall.
common_mistake: Arching the back or letting wrists/elbows leave the wall to cheat.
evidence_note: No source read for wall angels. Blanpied 2017 supports scapulothoracic strengthening for patients with neck pain only, not this exercise.

Repeat smoothly 8 times.

name: Tendon gliding (finger fist series)
duration_reps: 5 cycles per hand, 3 s per position (AAOS: 5-10 reps, 2-3x/day)
steps: Start with the hand in front of you, wrist straight, fingers fully straight.
Bend only the fingertips into a hook with the knuckles pointing up; hold about 3 s.
Make a tight fist with the thumb over the fingers; hold about 3 s.
Open the hand back to straight fingers. Repeat 5 cycles per hand, slow and smooth.
key_cue: Move through each position slowly, 3 s each.
common_mistake: Forcing a tight fist through pain.
evidence_note: AAOS OrthoInfo handout (read) lists tendon glides for people with carpal tunnel syndrome, to be done under clinician supervision; gentle pulling is expected but not increased pain. Benefit for prevention in healthy typists is unproven.

name: Median nerve glide (arm-and-wrist nerve slider)
duration_reps: 5-10 reps, about 3 s per position (AAOS: 3-7 s holds, 10-15 reps/day, for patients)
steps: Sit tall. Make a loose fist with the thumb outside the fingers.
Extend the fingers, keeping the thumb close to the side of the hand.
Keep the fingers straight and extend the wrist (hand bent back toward the forearm); then extend the thumb.

Keeping all that, turn the forearm palm up; optionally use the other hand to gently stretch the thumb, with very light pressure. Hold each position about 3 s; return to the fist and repeat slowly, 5-10 times; switch arms. Stay below any tingling.
key_cue: Gliding, not stretching: stay below a mild sensation, and never reach tingling.
common_mistake: Pushing into numbness/tingling or pulling hard on the thumb.
evidence_note: AAOS handout (read) lists median nerve glides for carpal tunnel syndrome, supervised by a clinician; evidence of effect is limited. Included only as a gentle optional exercise.

sources.title: AAOS OrthoInfo: Therapeutic exercise program for carpal tunnel syndrome
sources.verification: PDF unreadable by fetch tool; tendon glide (3 s holds) and median nerve glide (3-7 s holds, 10-15 reps) details from search summary only. Intended for people with carpal tunnel syndrome

contraindications_safety: Stop with tingling, numbness, burning or pain. Avoid if you have acute nerve symptoms, recent injury, or are pregnant with carpal tunnel and told otherwise. Seek care if hand symptoms persist.
verification_note: AAOS handout (read): 6 positions: fist with thumb OUTSIDE fingers; extend fingers keeping thumb at side; extend wrist; extend thumb; turn forearm palm up; use other hand to gently stretch the thumb (not too much pressure). Hold each 3-7 s, 10-15 reps a day. Catalog steps differ (thumb 'tucked beside', no separate thumb extension). Rewritten to the AAOS sequence. AAOS says exercises are for CTS under doctor supervision; AAOS tells patients to call if numbness steadily worsens. 'Never reach tingling' is the app's conservative rule. Recommend marking this as an optional, not default, exercise.

name: Prayer stretch and finger spreads
duration_reps: 3 reps x 5-7 s hold, then 5 finger spreads
steps: Sit with elbows on the desk and palms together in front of the chest.
Slowly lower the wrists toward the desk, keeping palms together, until a mild stretch; hold 5-7 s (CCOHS).
Release, shake out the hands gently.
Spread the fingers wide for 3 s, then relax; repeat 5 times.
key_cue: Keep the palms together as the wrists lower.
common_mistake: Forcing the wrists into pain.
evidence_note: CCOHS 'palms together wrist lower' (5-7 s x3).

sources.title: CCOHS: Office Ergonomics - Stretching at the Workstation
sources.verification: page read in full

contraindications_safety: Stop with pain, numbness or tingling. Caution with carpal tunnel, arthritis, recent injury.
verification_note: CCOHS (read): palms together, hold 5 to 7 s, relax, repeat 3 times. Matches. Finger spreads are an app addition (no source, harmless).

name: 20-20-20 eye break
duration_reps: 20 s, every 20 min of screen time
steps: Stop typing and lean back slightly, hands off the keyboard.
Choose an object at least 6 m (20 feet) away, for example through a window.
Look at it for 20 s; breathe and blink fully and softly several times.
Return to the screen.
key_cue: Look far and blink, do not just stare at a distant spot.
common_mistake: Looking at another near screen (phone) during the break.
evidence_note: Rule is popularly attributed to optometrist Jeffrey Anshel (origin NOT verified in this research). AAO's computer-use page does not mention the rule. Only study found (Talens-Estarelles 2022, n=29, no control, no randomization) showed short-lived symptom reduction while reminders were active; it is not an RCT. A 'Johnson & Shi' trial could not be located and is NOT cited. Rule is low-risk and plausibly useful mainly because it prompts breaks and blinking.

sources.title: Talens-Estarelles et al. 2022/2023, Cont Lens Anterior Eye: The effects of breaks on digital eye strain, dry eye and binocular vision: testing the 20-20-20 rule
sources.verification: abstract read; n=29, single group before/after, NO control and NO randomization (it is not an RCT); symptoms improved at 2 weeks, gain not kept 1 week after reminders stopped

sources.title: American Academy of Ophthalmology: Computer use and eye strain
sources.verification: page read in full; it does NOT mention the 20-20-20 rule; it recommends conscious blinking (about 15/min normal vs 5-7/min at computers)

contraindications_safety: Safe for nearly everyone. Persistent eye pain, sudden vision change, flashes or floaters: see an eye professional. Break also suits people with eyestrain from non-screen close work.
verification_note: Talens-Estarelles C et al., Cont Lens Anterior Eye 2023;46(2), PMID 35963776 (online 2022): 29 symptomatic computer users, software with webcam gaze/blink monitoring and enforced break reminders, assessed before/after 2 weeks and 1 week after stopping; no control group, non-randomised (AOP report of the study, read); symptoms (dryness, sensitivity, discomfort) fell but returned to prior levels after reminders stopped. A Letter to the Editor and Response were published Oct 2023 (PubMed listing). AAO computer-use page (read): 'about 15 times in one minute' normal vs '5 to 7 times' at screens; no named 20-20-20 rule; recommends looking at a distant object periodically. The rule is conventionally attributed to the American Optometric Association/Anshel (search result, not verified). Catalog statements are accurate. Abstract itself not directly readable (PubMed cookie wall, ScienceDirect 403).

name: Eye palming (warm-hand relaxation)
steps: Wash your hands first (no sanitizer or lotion residue on the palms), then rub the palms together for about 5 s to warm them.
Close the eyes and cup the palms over them, fingers on the forehead, with no contact or pressure on the eyeballs.
Rest elbows on the desk; breathe slowly for 30-60 s.
Lower the hands and open the eyes slowly; blink.
key_cue: Cup, do not press; no pressure on the eyeballs.
common_mistake: Pressing on the eyes.
evidence_note: No authoritative page read confirms benefit. Palming derives from the Bates method, which has no controlled-trial support (search snippets). Kept only as a relaxation/rest break.

sources.title: American Academy of Ophthalmology: Computer use and eye strain
sources.verification: page read in full; it does NOT mention the 20-20-20 rule; it recommends conscious blinking (about 15/min normal vs 5-7/min at computers)

contraindications_safety: Never press on the eyeballs. Skip with an active eye infection, recent eye surgery or injury, or if you have been told by an eye professional to avoid touching the eye area. Use clean hands only; stop if pain or irritation.
verification_note: No authoritative source for benefit; Bates-derived, and search results report no controlled trial evidence for the Bates method. Harmless as a rest break if done as cupping without pressure. Contraindication wording tightened: reason is hygiene and pressure, not glaucoma per se. Keep as 'general guidance' or drop.

name: Blink reset (full blinks)
steps: Look away from the screen; relax the face.
Close the eyes slowly and fully over about 1 s; squeeze lightly for 1 s.
Open slowly; repeat 10 times at a relaxed pace.
Resume work, consciously blinking more often.
key_cue: Full closures, not half blinks.
common_mistake: Squeezing hard or rapid fluttering.
evidence_note: AAO: normal ~15 blinks/min versus 5-7 at computers; advises consciously blinking. No trial of this specific exercise read.

sources.title: American Academy of Ophthalmology: Computer use and eye strain
sources.verification: page read in full; it does NOT mention the 20-20-20 rule; it recommends conscious blinking (about 15/min normal vs 5-7/min at computers)

contraindications_safety: Stop if eye pain or irritation. Persistent dry-eye symptoms: consult an eye professional.
verification_note: AAO (read): normal about 15 blinks/min vs 5 to 7 at screens; advises blinking consciously. The 10-blink protocol and 'squeeze lightly 1 s' are app-chosen; keep the squeeze gentle.

name: Chair sit-to-stand (squat to chair)
steps: Sit near the front edge of a stable chair, feet hip-width, arms crossed over the chest or hovering for balance.
Lean slightly forward and stand up fully over about 2 s, squeezing the glutes at the top.
Lower slowly over 3 s until lightly touching the seat.
Repeat 8-10 times.
key_cue: Knees track over the toes; chest up; control the way down.
common_mistake: Collapsing onto the seat; knees caving inward; using a chair with wheels.
evidence_note: WHO 2020 recommends muscle-strengthening activity on 2+ days/week and breaking up sedentary time (the 8-10 rep desk dose is not a tested prescription). Sit-to-stand is a validated functional movement.

sources.title: Bull et al. 2020, BJSM: WHO guidelines on physical activity and sedentary behaviour
sources.verification: search summary only; 150-300 min/wk moderate activity, muscle strengthening on 2+ days/wk, limit sedentary time (no numeric threshold)

sources.title: Cornell (A. Hedge): reminder software, micro-breaks, 3-S method (sit 20, stand 8, stretch 2 min)
sources.verification: search summary only

contraindications_safety: Use a non-wheeled, stable chair (or wall behind it). Stop with chest pain, dizziness, knee/hip pain. Caution with knee or hip replacement, balance problems, and heart or blood-pressure conditions. Can sweat slightly; lower intensity if needed.
verification_note: WHO 2020 (Bull et al., BJSM 54:1451-1462, search summary): muscle-strengthening on 2+ days/week at moderate or greater intensity; reduce sedentary behaviour; evidence insufficient for a numeric sedentary threshold. Class-level only; the 8-10 rep dose is app-chosen. Cornell 3-S (sit 20, stand 8, stretch 2 min; Hedge, search snippet) concerns sit/stand patterns, not this exercise. Typo 'using wheels chair' fixed.

name: Desk (incline) push-up
posture: standing at sturdy desk or wall
steps: Place hands on the edge of a sturdy desk (or wall), slightly wider than shoulder width; step back until the body is a straight diagonal line.
Brace the core, bend the elbows to about 45 degrees from the body and lower the chest toward the desk over 2 s.
Pause briefly; press back up over 1-2 s.
Repeat 8-10 times; a wall is easier, a lower desk is harder.
key_cue: Straight line from head to heels; elbows at about 45 degrees.
common_mistake: Sagging hips; flaring elbows; unstable desk or wheeled furniture.
evidence_note: Upper-body strengthening falls under WHO muscle-strengthening recommendations (class-level only).

sources.title: Bull et al. 2020, BJSM: WHO guidelines on physical activity and sedentary behaviour
sources.verification: search summary only; 150-300 min/wk moderate activity, muscle strengthening on 2+ days/wk, limit sedentary time (no numeric threshold)

contraindications_safety: Skip or use a wall with shoulder, wrist or elbow injury or carpal tunnel flare-ups. Make sure the desk is fixed. Stop with pain. Pregnancy: use a higher incline and avoid pressure on the abdomen. Mild exertion; may cause slight sweating.
verification_note: WHO 2020 class-level muscle strengthening only (search summary). Incline push-up mechanics are standard; dose app-chosen.

name: Wall sit
steps: Stand with back against a wall, feet about 60 cm from the wall, hip-width apart.
Slide down until the knees are bent about 60-90 degrees (only as low as comfortable); knees above ankles.
Hold 20-30 s, arms crossed or hanging, breathing steadily.
Slide back up; rest 20 s; repeat once.
key_cue: Knees stacked over ankles; back flat on the wall.
common_mistake: Holding the breath; going too deep too soon; pressing hands on thighs.
evidence_note: Falls under WHO muscle-strengthening class recommendations; isometric holds are also noted as BP-sensitive in clinical practice.

sources.title: Bull et al. 2020, BJSM: WHO guidelines on physical activity and sedentary behaviour
sources.verification: search summary only; 150-300 min/wk moderate activity, muscle strengthening on 2+ days/wk, limit sedentary time (no numeric threshold)

contraindications_safety: Do not go deeper than 90 degrees of knee bend; use a shallower angle with knee pain or patellofemoral issues. Breathe steadily throughout (no breath-holding). With high blood pressure that is uncontrolled, heart disease or dizziness, check with a clinician before isometric holds. Stop with chest pain, dizziness or sharp pain. Can cause leg burn and sweat.
verification_note: Hypertension wording corrected: isometric holds acutely raise BP, mostly through breath-holding (Valsalva); isometric training is also studied as a BP-LOWERING therapy (handgrip RCTs, search snippets). So the rule is: breathe throughout, and people with uncontrolled hypertension or heart disease should check with a clinician. Knee angle: stay at or above 90 degrees of knee bend (patellofemoral load rises beyond that; trainer/health sources, search snippets). Dose 20-30 s consistent with beginner programming from NASM blog snippet. Class-level WHO support only.

name: Standing calf raises
steps: Stand with feet hip-width, a hand lightly on the desk for balance.
Rise onto the balls of the feet over 2 s, lifting the heels as high as comfortable.
Hold 1 s at the top.
Lower slowly over 3 s. Repeat 12-15 times.
key_cue: Rise straight up; do not roll the ankles outward.
common_mistake: Bouncing quickly; rolling ankles out.
evidence_note: WHO class-level muscle-strengthening; circulation benefit during sitting is plausible but not verified here. NHS calf stretch is a related flexibility exercise.

sources.title: Bull et al. 2020, BJSM: WHO guidelines on physical activity and sedentary behaviour
sources.verification: search summary only; 150-300 min/wk moderate activity, muscle strengthening on 2+ days/wk, limit sedentary time (no numeric threshold)

sources.title: NHS: Flexibility exercises (neck rotation, neck stretch, sideways bend, calf stretch)
sources.verification: page read in full

contraindications_safety: Hold support if balance is limited. Stop with calf cramps, Achilles pain or dizziness. Caution after Achilles injury.
verification_note: No specific source for the 12-15 rep dose; WHO class-level muscle-strengthening only; the circulation benefit is not verified and is not claimed. Mechanics are standard and low risk.

name: Marching in place
steps: Stand tall, arms bent at the sides.
March in place, lifting each knee to about hip height or comfortable height; opposite arm swings forward.
Keep a steady rhythm, about 100 steps per minute, soft landings.
Slow down gradually for the last 10 s.
key_cue: Tall posture, quiet footsteps.
common_mistake: Slouching; stomping loudly.
evidence_note: WHO 2020: some activity is better than none; reduce sedentary time (no specific threshold). Light activity breaks improve cardiometabolic markers in trials not fetched here.

sources.title: Bull et al. 2020, BJSM: WHO guidelines on physical activity and sedentary behaviour
sources.verification: search summary only; 150-300 min/wk moderate activity, muscle strengthening on 2+ days/wk, limit sedentary time (no numeric threshold)

sources.title: Cornell (A. Hedge): reminder software, micro-breaks, 3-S method (sit 20, stand 8, stretch 2 min)
sources.verification: search summary only

contraindications_safety: Use supportive shoes; stop with chest pain, dizziness, shortness of breath. Caution with balance issues or cardiac conditions. Quiet; mild sweat at most.
verification_note: WHO 2020 (search summary): some activity is better than none; 150-300 min/week moderate activity. 100 steps/min as a moderate cadence is common in the literature but was not read here; the catalog states it only as 'about'. Duran et al. 2023 (MSSE, n=11, lab) supports light-activity breaks of 5 min every 30 min (search snippet).

name: 5-minute walk
steps: Stand up and leave the desk, taking your phone or nothing.
Walk at a comfortable brisk pace, around the office, outside or up/down a corridor.
Keep shoulders loose, arms swinging, chin level.
Return and sit with a relaxed posture.
key_cue: Comfortable, brisk pace where you can still talk.
common_mistake: Staring at a phone while walking.
evidence_note: WHO 2020 supports reducing sedentary behaviour and 150-300 min/wk of moderate activity; Cornell's 3-S plan advocates regular standing/moving breaks.

sources.title: Bull et al. 2020, BJSM: WHO guidelines on physical activity and sedentary behaviour
sources.verification: search summary only; 150-300 min/wk moderate activity, muscle strengthening on 2+ days/wk, limit sedentary time (no numeric threshold)

sources.title: Cornell (A. Hedge): reminder software, micro-breaks, 3-S method (sit 20, stand 8, stretch 2 min)
sources.verification: search summary only

contraindications_safety: Stop with chest pain, dizziness or breathlessness; people with cardiovascular, balance, or joint conditions should adjust. Choose safe surfaces.
verification_note: Supported by WHO 2020 (class-level) and by Duran et al. 2023, Med Sci Sports Exerc: 11 middle/older-aged adults, 8 h lab conditions; 5-min walking breaks every 30 min attenuated glucose and lowered systolic BP most (search snippets; small sample, lab). Added as a source note.

name: Stair climbing
steps: Go to a stairwell; hold the handrail.
Climb at a steady pace, placing the whole foot on each step.
Descend carefully, one step at a time, hand on the rail.
Repeat for 2-5 min; slow down gently.
key_cue: Whole foot on each step; use the rail.
common_mistake: Rushing or skipping steps; looking at a phone on stairs.
evidence_note: Counts toward moderate-to-vigorous activity in WHO 2020 (class level); micro-dose benefit not fetched here.

sources.title: Bull et al. 2020, BJSM: WHO guidelines on physical activity and sedentary behaviour
sources.verification: search summary only; 150-300 min/wk moderate activity, muscle strengthening on 2+ days/wk, limit sedentary time (no numeric threshold)

contraindications_safety: Avoid with knee/hip pain, balance problems, vertigo or cardiac conditions; stop with chest pain or dizziness. Falls risk on stairs. Will raise heart rate and may cause sweat (office-friendly 1).
verification_note: WHO 2020 class-level (moderate-to-vigorous activity). Safety note is adequate (rail, cardiac, vertigo, falls). No micro-dose source read.
